intro: Five long reads for a slow Thursday: how China's city halls became venture funds, a human team that beat OpenAI to a landmark proof by days, why firms thinking with the same AI models are losing their edge, what the Odyssey teaches a rootless age, and why AI has made propagandists more efficient but not more persuasive.

stories.headline: China's real planners sit in city halls
stories.dek: Robin Rivaton and Ben Southwood argue that China's industrial rise owes less to Beijing's commands than to thousands of local governments run like venture funds competing for growth.
body: Imagine Y Combinator, the Silicon Valley start-up accelerator, put in charge of San Francisco. It would build transit aggressively, let developers pile up housing near the jobs and cut taxes to lure founders, because its returns would depend on the companies in its portfolio growing. That, Robin Rivaton and Ben Southwood write in Works in Progress, is roughly how a Chinese city government behaves.

The usual Western story about China's industrial ascent is one of central planning: Beijing picks sectors, pours in subsidies and directs state banks. The authors do not deny the subsidies, but they relocate the action. According to the IMF, subnational governments account for about 85% of Chinese public spending. Mayors and party secretaries in places such as Hefei and Hangzhou are judged on whether their local economic portfolios grow, and are promoted or sidelined accordingly. Beijing writes the rules and sets the prizes; the provinces, cities and counties compete to win them.

Their conclusion is pointed. The lesson for America and Europe is not to copy Chinese top-down planning, which is not really how China works, but to rediscover their own mid-century tradition of locally driven growth.
## Local heroes

Many of China's best-known manufacturers grew out of local initiative rather than national design. Huawei, BYD and DJI emerged from Shenzhen's Special Economic Zone, where officials had regulatory room to experiment. Geely, which began by making refrigerator parts, was quietly backed by Zhejiang province at a time when only designated firms were allowed to build cars. Beijing supported strategic sectors such as batteries, electronics and electric vehicles with subsidies, tax rebates and sales-tax exemptions, but it did not choose the winners.

Hefei is the central case. In 2008 the city put about $500m, almost a tenth of its revenue that year, into BOE Technology to build an LCD production line, taking an 81% stake in a subsidiary. BOE became the world's largest maker of display panels, supplying roughly a quarter of smartphone screens. In 2020 Hefei backed the carmaker NIO for a 24% stake, earning an internal rate of return above 30%. Over the decade to 2023 the city invested around $25bn of public money and reported earnings near $9bn.

Other cities tell similar stories. Wuhu built a carmaker from an imported engine line, poached engineers from the state automaker FAW and copied a Volkswagen design; the result was Chery, in which the city still holds a 21% stake worth about $3.7bn. In Ningde, in Fujian, local leaders gave the young battery firm CATL land, infrastructure, tax support and help attracting suppliers. Its bases there can now produce 330 gigawatt-hours a year, close to half of global demand for electric-vehicle batteries in 2023.
## Promotion as incentive

Why do officials behave like investors? Because their careers depend on it. Each official is assessed in a confidential file covering an entire career, and superiors evaluate juniors all the way down to village level. Economic metrics, including GDP per head, local revenue, investment and exports, weigh heavily. In one Shaoxing assessment the authors cite, 54 of 100 points related to economic development. In the 2000s, officials who delivered growth 3.3 percentage points above their predecessors were 40-50% more likely to be promoted, while failure could mean demotion or early retirement.

Money reinforces ambition. After 1980 provinces kept about 75 of every 100 marginal yuan they raised; by 1990 the average retention rate was close to 90%. Later reforms cut their VAT share but left them almost all revenue from selling land-use rights.

The career of Li Qiang, now China's second-ranking leader, illustrates the model. As party secretary of Wenzhou from 2002 he encouraged private firms and private investment in infrastructure, and the city's GDP grew by 14.8% and 14.1% in his first two years. As governor of Zhejiang he reportedly cut more than 700 approval requirements. Chinese officials, the authors argue, resemble company directors more than administrators.
## Building clusters

Competition among many local planners means that winning strategies get copied and scaled. Crucially, Chinese local governments capture the spillovers of growth through rising land values and tax receipts, which gives them a reason to supply the public goods firms need. The Bay Area, by contrast, is divided among 101 municipal governments, and many Western cities face property-tax rules that limit what they gain when their economies boom.

Anchor firms are a favoured tool. To win Tesla's Shanghai factory, the city offered about $289m in grants, arranged $2.2bn in cheap loans, cut corporate tax by ten points from 2019 to 2023 and sold 86 hectares of land at half price. The plant was ready roughly two years faster than retooling at Tesla's Fremont site would have taken. China spends about 2% of GDP on cash subsidies, the authors note, against roughly 0.3% in America and 0.5% in the EU. Cities zone cheap industrial land and recoup the cost by selling other land to developers.

Kunshan shows how far this can go. Once a poor county, it built an industrial zone in the mid-1980s without Beijing's permission, then courted Taiwanese electronics firms with schools, media and cheap land. Firms including Foxconn and Acer Peripherals arrived, and by the late 2000s Kunshan made half the world's laptops. Specialised clusters abound: Danyang's 1,600 companies make half the world's spectacle lenses. Official data show 4.1m manufacturing enterprises by 2023, about 20 times the American count, 96% of them privately owned.
## Cheap capital and its costs

Beijing's first job is feeding the machines with capital. It restricts outward investment, including a $50,000 annual cap on what individuals can move abroad, and holds down deposit rates. Household deposits reached about 165trn yuan in September 2025, roughly 122% of GDP, while typical current-account rates were 0.15% in early 2025. Corporate debt is around 138% of GDP, yet financing costs are under 1% of industrial firms' turnover.

The authors are candid about the waste. The car industry could build 55.5m vehicles a year but used only about half that capacity in 2024, whereas Western plants usually run above 80%. BYD's profit margin is around 4%, and China's capital efficiency is about half America's. Beijing's second job is therefore to curb overcapacity, as it did in steel after output nearly doubled between 2006 and 2015. Its third is policing the tournament against local protectionism, hence its recent push for a unified national market. Until 2013 officials also routinely inflated GDP figures: younger mayors reported growth 3.4 points higher than older peers, a gap that night-time lights and electricity use did not confirm. Corruption flourished too, though the authors judge that much of it greased deals rather than draining the economy.
## The Chicago way

The final turn is the most provocative. China today, the authors argue, resembles America in the 1950s and 1960s, when property taxes made up 87% of local tax income and roughly 70% of local revenue was raised locally. Mayors such as Richard Daley in Chicago and William Hartsfield in Atlanta, and builders such as Robert Moses in New York, chased growth because voters rewarded it. Those growth machines have largely stalled, Houston and Nashville being exceptions. The West, the authors conclude, does not need a new model; it needs to revive its old one.
stories.counterpoint: The model's successes are visible while its failures are buried in local debt, ghost factories and land-sale finance that collapsed with the property market. Rewarding officials on GDP also produced fake statistics and environmental damage, and the system works partly because it lacks democratic veto points that Western societies value. Reviving 1950s-style growth machines would also revive the bulldozer politics that produced the backlash against Moses in the first place.
stories.why: Western debates about China tend to swing between fear of an all-seeing planner and confidence that state direction must fail. This essay offers a more useful frame: decentralised competition under hard incentives. It also turns the question back on the West, asking why its own cities so rarely gain from the growth they host.
questions: What would change in your own city if its leaders captured a share of the value created by local growth?
Is it possible to reward officials for growth without also rewarding them for gaming the numbers?
Which Western institutions, if any, still behave like the mid-century growth machines the authors describe?

stories.headline: Mathematicians race the machines, and just win
stories.dek: Rumours that OpenAI had cracked the unique games conjecture sent three MIT researchers scrambling to post a landmark human result first, and raised hard questions about what AI does to the practice of mathematics.
body: On the morning of September 11th Dor Minzer, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and one of the leading experts on a famous problem in computer science called the unique games conjecture, got a text from a friend asking whether he was about to settle it. He assumed it was a joke. Then more messages arrived, and the rumours converged: OpenAI, which had recently announced a striking proof about the behaviour of fluids, supposedly had a proof of the conjecture and might publish soon.

Minzer had not proved it. But he and two graduate students, Yumou Fei and Shuo Wang, had recently proved a major result about a close relative of the conjecture, and they were still writing it up, a process that normally takes months. They rushed. Three days later they posted a 95-page paper whose first page carried a disclaimer: the manuscript was mathematically complete but not in the form the authors wanted to share. On October 6th OpenAI duly announced its own proof of the unique games conjecture.
Ben Brubaker's report in Quanta tells the story of both results, and of a field unsettled by the arrival of machines that can do its hardest work.
## What the conjecture says

The conjecture concerns constraint satisfaction problems, the family of puzzles that includes sudoku and the seating plan at a wedding. Some have a perfect solution that is very hard to find; others have no perfect solution at all, and the best one can do is satisfy as many constraints as possible. Complexity theorists want to know where the line falls between approximations that are easy to find and those that are hopelessly hard.

Subhash Khot proposed the unique games conjecture in 2002, while still a graduate student. It concerns a graph-colouring version of the problem, in which each edge carries a rule about how the colours at its two ends must relate. Suppose the best possible colouring satisfies 99% of the rules. Intuition says that settling for 1%, or 0.001%, ought to be much easier. The conjecture says intuition is wrong: however far you lower your standards, some instances remain intractable.

Its importance comes from its connections. Researchers have used it to study the geometry of foams and the properties of voting systems. In 2008 Prasad Raghavendra showed that if the conjecture holds, a particular classic algorithm is the best possible approach for every constraint satisfaction problem that lacks a perfect solution. A proof would show that current methods for a vast range of problems cannot be improved, moving the field towards a unified theory of computational difficulty.
## The blind spot

The conjecture has a gap, which Khot recognised from the start. It speaks only about cases where the best solution satisfies most, but not all, constraints. It says nothing about problems where a perfect solution exists. To cover these he defined a variant, the 2-to-1 games problem, in which each rule permits two colours rather than one, and conjectured that some instances have a perfect solution that is nonetheless hard to approximate even to tiny fractions.

Minzer played a leading role in a 2018 result that the article describes as the first significant advance towards proving Khot's conjectures. Progress then stalled. In 2025 he offered two problems to Fei and Wang, who had just finished their first year of graduate school. They chose the 2-to-1 problem.
## Months of failure, then a fit

The strategy was to link the 2-to-1 problem to one whose difficulty was already understood. Earlier work had turned graph colouring into a question about error-correcting codes. Fei and Wang found a promising new family of codes but could not see how to join it to the other pieces the proof required. Months of attempts failed; Fei likened the task to forcing a circle and a triangle together in a jigsaw. In April 2026 the team finally succeeded by combining the new code with five approaches that had each failed on their own.

What they proved is slightly weaker than Khot's statement: a 4-to-1 version, with four colour options per rule instead of two. Many consequences of the conjecture still follow. The most striking concerns a classic problem in which neighbouring nodes must simply receive different colours. It was already known that when a graph can be coloured with three colours, actually finding such a colouring can be prohibitively hard. The new result implies that even with any number of extra colours allowed, some graphs remain hard to colour. Mark Braverman of Princeton put it vividly: it cannot be done even with the whole Crayola box. Computer scientists had sought this result for decades.
The paper is rough. Minzer admits that from section 6 onward it has almost no connecting prose, and the authors apologise for it; a revised version is planned.
## The machine's announcement

OpenAI's October 6th release claimed a proof of the unique games conjecture itself, alongside 376 other results across mathematics, including 40 further proofs in theoretical computer science. It also included a proof of the 2-to-1 conjecture checked in Lean, a formal proof-verification language. Brubaker calls it the highest-profile AI-generated proof in the field so far, but notes that the manuscript had been neither edited by humans nor reviewed by independent experts when he wrote.

Reactions to the flood of machine proofs mixed alarm with curiosity. Reactions to Minzer's paper were simpler. Ryan O'Donnell of Carnegie Mellon called it another truly great result, and praised the authors for solving the problem and writing it up themselves. Braverman was sharper about the manner of the AI announcement, warning that mathematics by press release is unhealthy and that the uncertainty is already taking a toll. Yet he also saw promise: if researchers can identify the key assumptions in an AI proof, which is not always easy, they can vary them and see what follows. It is not, in his view, one and done.
## What is lost

Minzer's worries run deeper. Failed attempts, he argues, are where researchers learn, and his own team's months of dead ends taught them a great deal. Tools that skip straight to the answer may remove that education. He also fears that AI will discourage ambitious, long-term projects. Humans need sleep and food and have moods; how, he asks, can anyone plan a multi-year assault on a problem knowing a trillion-dollar company might publish the answer first?

The article ends without resolving the question. For now, a human team got there just ahead. What happens when it does not, and when the machine's proof is correct but opaque, is the problem the field must now confront.
stories.counterpoint: Mathematics has absorbed computer-assisted proofs before, from the four-colour theorem onward, and the discipline adapted. If OpenAI's proofs check out in Lean, the result is more knowledge, not less, and researchers freed from grinding technical work may tackle bolder questions. Nostalgia for productive failure can shade into protecting a guild.
stories.why: The unique games conjecture sits at the centre of our understanding of what computers can and cannot do efficiently, so a proof would reshape a large body of theory. The episode is also an early, concrete look at how AI changes the incentives and rhythms of research: priority races, unreviewed claims and the question of whether understanding still requires struggle.
questions: If a machine proves a theorem that no human fully understands, has our knowledge actually grown?
How should credit and priority work when a company can release hundreds of results at once?
What kinds of learning in your own work come only from failure, and would you want a tool that removed them?

source.title: As AI Closed In on 'Unique Games' Proof, Researchers Raced to Beat the Machines
source.author: Ben Brubaker

stories.headline: When every company thinks with the same brain
stories.dek: Aaron Horwath argues that firms outsourcing their thinking to the same few AI models are straightening out the bends that once made them distinctive, and will eventually pay to put them back.
body: Lukas Weber is a 28-year-old copywriter at a mid-sized software company that has declared itself AI-first. He no longer writes much. Instead he manages a set of AI agents that research newsletter topics, draft copy, send proposals to website visitors, analyse campaign data and answer email. His team has shrunk, and his bosses expect him not to write at all. He says he could not go back to the old way of working, yet he misses producing something that is unmistakably his.

Aaron Horwath, who directs AI operations at a creative-technology company, opens his Noema essay with Weber as a representative figure (the essay does not say whether he is a real individual or a composite). The pattern, Horwath says, is spreading across HR, sales, customer success and engineering. Knowledge workers are handing over cognitive work, and because firms in the same industry lean on the same handful of large language models, the output converges. Distinctiveness erodes, and so does the value of a firm's own people.
He calls the condition "Airbrain", adapting the critic Kyle Chayka's notion of "Airspace".
## From Airspace to Airbrain

In a 2016 article and later in his book "Filterworld", Chayka described how coffee shops, bars, hotels and Airbnbs from Berlin to Brooklyn had converged on a single interchangeable aesthetic, shaped by platforms such as Instagram and Foursquare. Horwath argues that AI is now doing to knowledge work what algorithms did to interiors.

His first exhibit is small: the em dash, which LLMs use so heavily that many readers now treat it as a sign of machine-made slop. He cites reporting in the Wall Street Journal, a Reuters Institute analysis of how AI prose differs from human writing, and a 2025 Cornell study finding that AI suggestions make writing more generic. Designers have noticed the same thing in the purple-gradient websites AI tools keep producing.

The more serious evidence comes from a 2026 paper in PNAS Nexus by Emily Wenger of Duke and Yoed Kenett of the Technion. They set 22 commercial LLMs against more than 100 people on standard creativity tasks. Some models beat some individuals, but as a group the models converged on similar answers, while the humans did not. Wenger warned that heavy reliance would pull writing towards the same words and grammar.

Horwath stresses that the problem is not confined to marketing copy. Employees now use AI for strategy, sales coaching, stakeholder management and devising business solutions, the work that shapes how a company sees its market and how the market sees it.
## Straightening the river

The essay's central image comes from central Florida. In 1954 the Army Corps of Engineers set out to tame flooding along the Kissimmee river, which wound through 103 miles of bends. Between 1962 and 1971 it was straightened and dredged into a canal 30 feet deep. The floods stopped. But oxygen levels fell, nutrients built up and sediment poured into Lake Okeechobee. Nearly 35,000 acres of floodplain habitat vanished, along with about 90% of the wintering waterfowl, and the bass fishery gave way to bowfin and gar. Restoration began in 1999, put back 44 miles of bends, finished in 2021 and cost more than $1bn.

Horwath maps this on to the firm. The traditional route for an idea, from conception through stakeholder feedback, refinement and approval to resourcing, is slow and often maddening. But its meetings and arguments refined ideas and made them particular to the organisation. AI lets an individual contributor skip all of that and build alone. He likens the result to what McKinsey has described as an AI assembly line with humans as foremen, and argues that manufacturing logic suits production, not innovation. The bends served a purpose.

He leans on strategy scholarship for the competitive point. A firm's unique selling points come from the combined talent of its people; route everything through the same models and that talent is filtered out. Jay Barney of the University of Utah and co-authors, writing in MIT Sloan Management Review, argue that AI will homogenise rather than differentiate, precisely because the value it unlocks is available to everyone.
## Skills that wither

There is a second cost. Horwath cites a 2026 report in Nature finding that skills decline quickly once AI is introduced, and a GoTo survey of 2,500 employees in which 39% said their reliance on AI was making them less intelligent. Firms that later want human-generated work back may find the capability has atrophied and takes time to rebuild. The fastest adopters, he suggests, should prepare to become more selective: more AI in some places, deliberately restored human effort in others.
## The coming zag

Sameness, he predicts, eventually stops paying. In one study participants shown photographs of coffee shops could not reliably say where they were: none placed all six correctly, and only 6% could tell Chicago from San Francisco. Cafés have since begun chasing differentiated experiences. Horwath expects firms to make the same turn, and finds early signs in a 2024 Harvard Business Review piece on AI's failure to provide lasting advantage, in Deloitte's 2026 human-capital report locating advantage in adaptability and judgment, and in EY's reported $100m bonus programme for human skills.

He draws on a 2026 Cambridge paper by Erin McGurk and David Khachaturov proposing a barbell labour market: near-free AI output at one end, premium verifiably human work at the other, and a hollowed-out middle. Oversight roles drift to cheaper labour markets, while tastemakers and strategists command a premium. He notes that AI companies themselves, including Anthropic and OpenAI, are hiring for taste and brand roles.

The next temptation, he warns, will be to replace full-time staff with freelancers and fractional executives. Upwork reports skilled freelancing rising from 28% to 38% of skilled knowledge workers, and Gartner predicts that by 2027 more than 30% of midsize enterprises will retain at least one fractional executive. Horwath invokes Rory Sutherland's "doorman fallacy": a hotel doorman seems to exist to open doors, but he also provides security, recognition and status, and removing him destroys value that is hard to measure. An organisation of fractional workers, he argues, is barely an organisation.
## Choosing the friction

Horwath does not argue against AI; he concedes it may help firms move faster and is useful for many tasks. His point is that "AI for everything" is too blunt. Leaders must decide which roles stay human, where AI supports distinctive work, which areas should be kept free of it, and which friction is worth preserving. For people like Weber, he concludes, the path lies in cultivating taste, perspective and a voice of their own.
stories.counterpoint: Homogenisation may be a transitional phase rather than a destination: firms can fine-tune models on proprietary data, and the same tools that flatten prose can also widen the range of ideas a small team can test. Much of the evidence Horwath cites comes from consultancies and vendors with their own interests, and the slow consensus processes he romanticises also killed many good ideas.
stories.why: Most corporate AI strategy is still measured in hours saved, not in what makes a firm worth choosing. Horwath shifts the question to differentiation and organisational capability, which is where long-run returns are decided. His argument also applies to schools, churches and newsrooms that risk sounding exactly like each other.
questions: Which parts of your own work would you deliberately keep slow and human, and why?
How would you notice if your organisation's distinctive judgment were slowly being replaced by a model's defaults?
Is a voice developed with constant AI assistance still recognisably your own?

source.title: Now Entering: The Era Of Bleh
source.author: Aaron Horwath

stories.headline: What Odysseus teaches a rootless age
stories.dek: Stephen Pimentel reads the Odyssey as a manual of governance and identity for societies that have lost their names, fathers and homes, and argues that its strangeness is the point.
body: The Odyssey opens by naming its subject: a man of many turns, who suffered much on the sea while trying to bring himself and his companions home. In a few lines the proem sets out the poem's concerns, intelligence, politics, suffering and return, and introduces a hero defined less by rank or raw courage than by the versatile use of his mind.

Stephen Pimentel's essay in Palladium argues that Homer's poem is not merely a monument of Western literature but a living account of human nature and of the habits of mind that governing well requires. Its lessons, he contends, matter more now than they did a generation ago, because modern life has loosened the inherited bonds of name, family and place that the poem takes for granted. Civilisation, on this reading, does not maintain itself; it must be recovered through memory, intelligence, strength and the stubborn desire to go home.
The poem presents human beings as mortals placed between beasts and gods: shaped by bonds they did not choose, yet able to judge them, and responsible for action amid forces they cannot control.
## Reading the alien

Pimentel warns against two opposite mistakes. One treats Homer's Greeks as primitive versions of ourselves; the other treats them as wholly inaccessible. He identifies four features modern readers find foreign. The gods are real and partisan: Athena admires Odysseus's cunning, while Poseidon pursues him out of spite. Human responsibility coexists with divine action; early in the poem Zeus rebukes mortals for blaming the gods for suffering they bring on themselves, and Odysseus's men die after ignoring a divine warning about the cattle of Helios. Ethics rest on hierarchy, honour and shame within concrete relationships, not on universal equality. And retribution is part of justice, with Orestes's killing of Aegisthus held up as a model.

Modern adaptations, he complains, tend to soften these features or overwrite them with themes such as trauma and psychological recovery. That is a loss, because the poem's alienness is what stops readers from absorbing it too easily into their own assumptions.
## A displaced man

Odysseus loses his name, his father, his land and his household, and his homecoming is complete only when all four are restored. Pimentel links this to a modern homelessness that afflicts even people who own their houses.

The Polyphemus episode is his chief text on identity. Odysseus tells the Cyclops his name is Nobody, a trick that lets him escape. But he cannot bear anonymity, because his glory depends on being named in song, so as he sails away he shouts out who he is and brings Poseidon's wrath upon himself. Pimentel compares this to online anonymity, which evades accountability but forfeits recognition unless one unmasks.

Telemachus's remark that no man truly knows his own father points to a wider absence of fatherhood and political continuity. A reduced, nuclear view of fatherhood, Pimentel argues, breeds short-term thinking. Loyalty, meanwhile, appears where one might not expect it: Eumaeus the swineherd, a foreign-born slave, proves more faithful than Ithaca's native elites. Loyalty can be chosen, and betrayal can come from within one's own class.
## Excellence and judgment

Arete, usually translated as virtue, means excellence: the ability to perform a needed function well. Odysseus is polytropos, a man of many ways, and polymetis, of many skills. He adapts and improvises rather than relying on a single disposition, and Pimentel argues that excellence today requires the same flexibility in unfamiliar situations.

The Greeks faced mortality, strife, inequality and violence without illusions, rejecting the belief that the world is just. Odysseus returns not because his journey is safe but because he meets its dangers. He enters his own hall disguised as a beggar and delays his vengeance; Penelope holds off the suitors by weaving a shroud by day and unpicking it by night. Both show mastery of timing.

Pimentel sets this against what he calls post-Christian Western morality, with its stress on compassion, equality and safety. The Odyssey instead defends moral discrimination. Odysseus spares the bard and the herald only after confirming their innocence, and uses force against Polyphemus because the Cyclops has violated hospitality. He refuses Calypso's offer of immortality for a rugged home. The suitors' offences were deliberate and repeatedly warned against, so their punishment respects their agency. Yet Odysseus forbids his old nurse Eurycleia to exult over the dead, for justice does not license delight in killing.
## Three virtues

Pimentel singles out three qualities. Metis is practical cunning: knowing when to speak, hide, wait, test, strike or yield, as in the planning and execution of the escape from the Cyclops. Endurance, captured in the epithet polytlas, carries Odysseus through years on Calypso's island and abuse from his own servants; but suffering alone ennobles nothing, since his companions and the suitors suffer without gain, so endurance must be governed by its end. Memory binds a person to absent people and institutions. The lotus-eaters show that forgetting brings peace at the price of identity, while the recognition scenes, the scar Eurycleia finds, the bed only husband and wife know, the orchard trees his father Laertes once gave him, show identity as a life story written in body, place and deed.
## The poem of the future

Homer's images, Pimentel argues, shape perception more deeply than rules do: corrupt elites courting a queen, a beggar-king stringing a bow. Xenia, the reciprocal duties of host and guest, can be broken from either side, which distinguishes it from a one-directional humanitarianism. Telemachus addressing the assembly shows the limits of authority without power; Odysseus in rags shows that a leader must judge the true state of his authority, not its appearance. Shakespeare used the same device in Henry V on the eve of Agincourt.

When shared texts fade, he warns, judgment becomes literal and shallow, and societies lose the ability to tell hospitality from exploitation or retribution from sadism. He treats a recent Christopher Nolan film adaptation as a symptom, and points to the Bronze Age collapse of the twelfth century BC as a reminder that civilisations can fall. Pimentel does not urge a return to ancestral villages or old gods, and concedes that parts of Homer's world are repugnant to modern sensibilities. But he insists readers enter it on its own terms before judging. Odysseus returned to a poor, rugged Ithaca and rebuilt it. A vibrant, expansive civilisation is best; when that is out of reach, the second-best course is to battle all the way home.
stories.counterpoint: Pimentel's contrast between Homeric clarity and post-Christian softness is drawn with a broad brush; much of what he calls modern sentimentality descends from the Christian moral revolution that Homer's world lacked, and that revolution protected the weak in ways an honour culture rarely did. Reading a massacre of suitors as a model of justice also risks lending ancient prestige to contemporary political grievances.
stories.why: Debates about rootlessness, fatherhood and the decline of shared culture are usually conducted in sociology or polemic. Pimentel shows how an ancient text can supply images that sharpen judgment about leadership, loyalty and justice. For Christian readers, the essay is a useful foil: it raises the question of how the gospel both fulfils and overturns the honour ethic of the classical world.
questions: What are the name, father, land and household that anchor your own identity, and which feel most fragile?
Where is the line between righteous retribution and delight in another's ruin?
Which shared stories does your community still rely on to judge between hospitality and exploitation?

stories.headline: AI makes propagandists efficient, not persuasive
stories.dek: Renée DiResta finds that generative and agentic AI are transforming the back offices of state influence operations, while the evidence that they change anyone's mind remains thin.
body: In June OpenAI reported that accounts probably run by a Chinese technology contractor had falsely claimed that ChatGPT leaked user data, while another cluster used the chatbot to make political cartoons blaming American data centres for rising electricity bills. Republican lawmakers called for Justice Department investigations and the State Department weighed in. It was one of a string of disclosures: Iranian state propagandists using Claude to draft doctrine for influence campaigns, a former editor of Sputnik Moldova using AI to churn out articles and fabricated claims about Moldova's president before its 2025 election, a staffer at a Russian state outlet using it to write on-air captions.

Renée DiResta, a research professor at Georgetown's McCourt School of Public Policy and a contributing editor at Lawfare, has spent years studying such campaigns. Her essay surveys the threat reports now published by AI firms and platforms and reaches a deliberately two-sided verdict. AI clearly increases the capacity of influence operations. The evidence that those operations change public opinion is much weaker.
## Production and the back office

The reports show state-linked actors and commercial influence-for-hire firms using AI to write and translate content, invent personas, mimic target audiences and scale output. Quality improves as well as quantity: fewer of the tell-tale errors that once exposed operators, such as mangling African American Vernacular English while posing as Black Americans on X, slipping out of character or plagiarising. Iran, Russia and China recur throughout.

The more surprising finding, DiResta argues, is administrative. AI is reshaping the unglamorous work of audience research, scheduling, data processing and control software. The data-centre operators used ChatGPT to write code automating log-ins across platforms. This shift to back-office efficiency, she suggests, is a larger change than the content-production gains researchers had predicted.

History makes the point. The claim that Russia's Internet Research Agency spent "only $100,000 on Facebook ads" during 2015-17 is misleading: a Justice Department indictment shows its Project Lakhta budget exceeded $1.25m a month by September 2016. IRA staff visited America, ran internal reviews of organic engagement and pivoted failing accounts; one successful Christian meme page began life as a Kermit the Frog meme page. That is expensive management work, and AI cheapens it. Anthropic reportedly found Iranian propaganda institutions using Claude to produce doctrine manuals and planning documents that would otherwise have required a full programme office. In the Central African Republic, a coordinator for Politology, the Wagner Group's influence arm, used it to manage staff at a Wagner-founded radio station, drafting loyalty contracts, scoring reporters' articles and recommending dismissals.
## From generation to agents

DiResta distinguishes four kinds of AI work: generation, operational support such as background research and personal databases, workflow orchestration, and early autonomous execution. Her shorthand is that generative AI scales content while agentic AI scales operations. LKM Company, a French advertising agency, ran a pipeline producing text to exact specifications, down to character counts and internal links for search ranking, for roughly 70 fake local news sites. Operators aligned with the Iranian opposition group MEK ran a shared AI agent with memory files of banned words, approved sources and detection-evasion rules, so it kept producing without a human directing each session.

This matters because platform detection has long relied on spotting accounts that coordinate with one another. When coordination is embedded in the system, the operators need not coordinate at all, and the signal disappears.

Cyber operations show the same drift towards autonomy. Google reported Russian, Iranian and North Korean groups using Gemini for everything from password-spraying scripts to multilingual phishing lures. Anthropic described a Russia-linked actor whose agents checked whether security products had flagged its malware, then rebuilt it until it evaded detection again, a feedback loop that erodes the cost detection once imposed. Another operator used stolen API keys to sustain activity that once required a team, which makes sophistication a weaker clue to attribution. The link to influence is direct: the GRU's theft and release of Democratic emails in 2016 arguably shaped American debate more than IRA trolling did, and Anthropic reports a Russia-linked actor seizing the WhatsApp accounts of at least two former senior Ukrainian officials and exporting their chats, potential fuel for a hack-and-leak.
## Reach is the bottleneck

Production, DiResta stresses, is only the first hurdle. Operations must also achieve distribution and then effect. The successes she catalogues mostly ride on existing audiences: RT using AI to speed up an established newsroom, the Central African radio station broadcasting AI-assisted content daily to its listeners. LKM's network, by contrast, published nearly 9,000 articles in around 20 languages and drew almost no real engagement. OpenAI rated both China-linked campaigns at the bottom of its breakout scale, meaning neither spread beyond its own accounts. The data-centre accounts that alarmed Congress got essentially no reach.

The smarter operators know this. Russia-linked actors have paid established American influencers rather than build fake personas. The Chinese data-centre team planned slow cultivation of trustworthy everyday personas on Facebook, backed by ad spending. MEK operators trained an agent on about 8,400 posts from a real activist's Telegram account to hold live conversations impersonating him. A UAE-linked operation funded about 300 influencer accounts and treated their apparent independence as its main asset.

DiResta acknowledges studies published in Nature and Science last December showing that multi-turn conversations with chatbots can shift attitudes towards candidates and policies. But those experiments placed people in direct conversation with a bot, not scrolling past a sockpuppet's post in a crowded feed. She adds that influence can aim at agenda-setting, activation or intimidation rather than persuasion. The UAE-linked operation borrowed the identity of a real Sudanese human-rights group, ghost-wrote testimony for the UN Human Rights Council and compiled dossiers on UN special rapporteurs who criticised the Emirates.
## Power, not propaganda

The real objective, she argues, is power. Cheaper production lets states sustain more operations against more targets with fewer staff, building persistence even when most attempts fail. As content becomes abundant, the scarce assets become established accounts, credible intermediaries and trusted names, so she expects operators increasingly to buy, rent or impersonate real identities.

Her policy prescription is transparency across the whole chain from creation to distribution, plus researcher access to platform data. The trend runs the other way: Meta has moved to semi-annual reporting, and X's first disclosure of an inauthentic network in two years was a single post, three months after OpenAI reported the same campaign. Sharing between firms offers some hope; Anthropic reportedly uncovered a domestic astroturfing operation in Kenya after a tip from OpenAI.

Her caveats are central, not incidental. AI firms see production but lose sight of operations once they go live; platforms see distribution but not origins. Output does not prove reach, and reach does not prove influence. Much of the evidence is corporate self-reporting. The Iranian propagandists said they wanted to be the director rather than the narrator. AI makes directing cheaper, she concludes, but so far there is little sign it has made audiences easier to reach or persuade.
stories.counterpoint: Absence of measured persuasion is not absence of effect: the studies that could detect slow shifts in trust or turnout are rarely run, and the companies supplying the evidence have an interest in portraying misuse as ineffective. As agents learn to cultivate personas patiently, today's failed campaigns may simply be early iterations of more effective ones.
stories.why: Public debate swings between panic about AI-powered disinformation and dismissal of it. DiResta offers a sober framework, production, distribution and effect, that helps voters, regulators and journalists ask the right question about each scare. Her warning about trusted identities becoming the prize also bears on anyone whose name carries credibility.
questions: How would you know if your views on a contested issue had been shaped by a coordinated campaign?
Should AI companies be required to report misuse, or does that risk turning them into surveillance agencies?
If trusted voices become the scarcest resource in information warfare, what responsibilities do they carry?
